anomaly_def.Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level runtime parameters are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload mix, or version defaults, causing artificial bottlenecks that are not rooted in the true limits of the underlying resources.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage subsystem cannot sustain the read/write rate demanded by the workload, leading to saturated IOPS / bandwidth, deep I/O queues, and growing latency.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced limits on file handles, shared memory, threads, or other process quotas are exhausted, preventing the database from allocating additional OS resources even though engine-level limits might appear sufficient.

When all three anomalies are present simultaneously, symptoms overlap and amplify: checkpoint or log-flush storms triggered by bad configuration drive a surge of physical writes that immediately collide with an already bandwidth-bound storage layer, inflating write latency and pushing buffer-pool eviction and background flush waits sky-high. At the same time, the mounting backlog of I/O requests inflates kernel I/O contexts, file descriptors, and thread counts until OS quotas are hit, producing intermittent "cannot allocate" errors, failed worker spawns, or stalled client logins. Performance dashboards will show contradictory signals—CPU under-utilized, storage queues maxed out, and a rash of engine errors—making the root cause appear elusive. Batch windows stretch, OLTP transactions time out, and even read-only queries stall while waiting on dirty-page flushes that the storage device and OS can no longer service.

Causally, mis-set configuration parameters (e.g., too small checkpoint intervals, undersized log files, or excessive per-session work memory) act as the trigger that inflates I/O pressure well beyond normal steady-state. This sustained pressure forces the storage layer into throughput saturation, prolonging every I/O and keeping queue depths persistently high. The prolonged queues, in turn, require more kernel objects—threads, async-I/O contexts, file descriptors—which quickly consume the OS resource quotas. Once these limits are breached, the database engine can neither launch relief workers nor open additional files, so the mis-configuration and storage congestion self-reinforce, driving the system into a cascading slowdown that is far more severe than any of the three anomalies would cause in isolation.

entry.official_definition: The number of seconds to wait for more data from a connection before aborting the read.
entry.trigger_condition: The server waits for additional data from a connection longer than net_read_timeout.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
